steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the "Early episodes" section of an encyclopedia article on AI winters, covering the collapse of machine translation funding after the ALPAC report of 1966 and the abandonment of single-layer neural networks after 1969.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
### Machine translation and the ALPAC report of 1966
- Origins of NLP and machine translation; early excitement
- Media hype vs. the actual Georgetown–IBM demonstration
- Cold War government and CIA support
- Optimism, then word-sense disambiguation problems
- ALPAC report and end of funding
- Later path of machine translation
### The failure of single-layer neural networks in 1969
- Early networks abandoned in favor of symbolic AI
- Rosenblatt and perceptrons
- Minsky and Papert's Perceptrons
- Funding drought and revival

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
### Machine translation and the ALPAC report of 1966
- NLP roots early 1930s; began with machine translation (MT)
- real advances after Warren Weaver's memorandum, Machine translation of languages: fourteen essays, 1949
  - great excitement; IBM starts first machine; MIT first full-time MT professor; MT conferences
  - culmination: public Georgetown–IBM demonstration, 1954, wide newspaper coverage
- media exaggeration (as in all AI booms followed by winters)
  - headlines: "The bilingual machine", "Robot brain translates Russian into King's English", "Polyglot brainchild"
  - reality: curated set of only 49 Russian sentences; vocabulary 250 words
  - comparison: Paul Nation 2006 study, humans need 8,000 to 9,000-word families for 98% comprehension of written text
- Cold War: US government wants instant translation of Russian documents/scientific reports
  - aggressive government support from 1954
  - CIA interest, believed in MT, supported it; saw implications beyond CIA/intelligence community
- early optimism: Noam Chomsky's grammar work; "many predictions of imminent 'breakthroughs'"
  - underestimated word-sense disambiguation; machine needs to know what sentence is about
  - apocryphal example: "the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak" -> "the vodka is good but the meat is rotten"
  - later called the commonsense knowledge problem
- 1964: National Research Council concerned, forms ALPAC
  - famous 1966 report: MT more expensive, less accurate, slower than human translation
  - after some 20 million dollars, NRC ends all support; careers destroyed, research ended
- MT followed NLP: rule-based -> statistical -> neural networks -> large language models in 2023
### The failure of single-layer neural networks in 1969
- simple networks/circuits (Pitts and McCulloch's neural network for logic; Minsky's SNARC) failed, abandoned late 1950s
- symbol manipulation seemed more promising after Logic Theorist, General Problem Solver; logical reasoning seen as essence of intelligence
- perceptrons (Frank Rosenblatt) kept alive only by his personality
  - prediction: perceptron "may eventually be able to learn, make decisions, and translate languages"
- 1969 book Perceptrons (Minsky and Papert) stressed limits -> mainstream research ended
  - multilayered perceptrons not subject to criticism, but nobody in 1960s knew how to train them; backpropagation years away
- little major funding in 1970s and early 1980s; theoretical work continued
- winter ended mid 1980s: John Hopfield, David Rumelhart and others
- Rosenblatt died in boating accident shortly after Perceptrons published

### Machine translation and the ALPAC report of 1966

Natural language processing (NLP) research has roots in the early 1930s, and it began with the work on machine translation (MT). But significant advancements and applications started to appear after Warren Weaver published his influential memorandum, Machine translation of languages: fourteen essays, in 1949. The memorandum created great excitement in the research community. In the following years several notable things happened: IBM started developing the first machine, MIT appointed its first full-time professor in machine translation, and there were several conferences dedicated to MT. All of this culminated in the public demonstration of the Georgetown–IBM machine in 1954, which got widespread attention in respected newspapers.

Like all the AI booms that have been followed by desperate AI winters, the media tended to exaggerate how significant these developments were. Headlines about the Georgetown–IBM experiment used phrases like "The bilingual machine," "Robot brain translates Russian into King's English," and "Polyglot brainchild." But the actual demonstration was the translation of a curated set of only 49 Russian sentences into English, and the vocabulary of the machine was limited to just 250 words. To put this into perspective, a 2006 study by Paul Nation found that humans need a vocabulary of around 8,000 to 9,000-word families to comprehend written texts with 98% accuracy.

During the Cold War the US government was particularly interested in automatic, instant translation of Russian documents and scientific reports. Starting in 1954 the government aggressively supported machine translation efforts. Another factor that pushed mechanical translation forward was the interest of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). At that time the CIA firmly believed that developing machine translation capabilities was important and it supported such initiatives. The CIA also recognized that the program had implications that went beyond the interests of the CIA and the intelligence community.

  - apocryphal example: "the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak." -> "the vodka is good but the meat is rotten."
  - later: commonsense knowledge problem
- 1964: National Research Council forms ALPAC; 1966 report: MT more expensive, less accurate, slower than human translation
  - some 20 million dollars spent; NRC ends all support; careers destroyed, research ended
- MT path same as NLP: rule-based -> statistical -> neural networks -> large language models in 2023

### The failure of single-layer neural networks in 1969
- simple networks (Pitts and McCulloch's neural network for logic, Minsky's SNARC) abandoned late 1950s

steps.text:
### Machine translation and the ALPAC report of 1966

Natural language processing (NLP) research has roots in the early 1930s, and it began with the work on machine translation (MT). But significant advancements and applications started to appear after Warren Weaver published his influential memorandum, Machine translation of languages: fourteen essays, in 1949. The memorandum created great excitement in the research community. In the following years several notable things happened: IBM started developing the first machine, MIT appointed its first full-time professor in machine translation, and there were several conferences dedicated to MT. All of this culminated in the public demonstration of the Georgetown–IBM machine in 1954, which got widespread attention in respected newspapers.

Like all the AI booms that have been followed by desperate AI winters, the media tended to exaggerate how significant these developments were. Headlines about the Georgetown–IBM experiment used phrases like "The bilingual machine," "Robot brain translates Russian into King's English," and "Polyglot brainchild." But the actual demonstration was the translation of a curated set of only 49 Russian sentences into English, and the vocabulary of the machine was limited to just 250 words. To put this into perspective, a 2006 study by Paul Nation found that humans need a vocabulary of around 8,000 to 9,000-word families to comprehend written texts with 98% accuracy.

During the Cold War the US government was particularly interested in automatic, instant translation of Russian documents and scientific reports. Starting in 1954 the government aggressively supported machine translation efforts. Another factor that pushed mechanical translation forward was the interest of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). At that time the CIA firmly believed that developing machine translation capabilities was important and it supported such initiatives. The CIA also recognized that the program had implications that went beyond the interests of the CIA and the intelligence community.

At first the researchers were optimistic. Noam Chomsky's new work in grammar was streamlining the translation process, and there were "many predictions of imminent 'breakthroughs'". But the researchers had underestimated how profoundly difficult word-sense disambiguation was. To translate a sentence a machine needed to have some idea of what the sentence was about, and otherwise it made mistakes. An apocryphal example is "the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak." When it was translated back and forth with Russian, it became "the vodka is good but the meat is rotten." Later researchers would call this the commonsense knowledge problem.

By 1964 the National Research Council had become concerned about the lack of progress, and it formed the Automatic Language Processing Advisory Committee (ALPAC) to look into the problem. In a famous 1966 report they concluded that machine translation was more expensive, less accurate and slower than human translation. After spending some 20 million dollars the NRC ended all support. Careers were destroyed and research ended.

Machine translation went down the same path as NLP, from rule-based approaches to statistical approaches and then to neural network approaches, which culminated in large language models in 2023.

### The failure of single-layer neural networks in 1969

Simple networks or circuits of connected units failed to deliver the results that were promised, and they were abandoned in the late 1950s. These included Walter Pitts and Warren McCulloch's neural network for logic and Marvin Minsky's SNARC system. After the success of programs like the Logic Theorist and the General Problem Solver, algorithms that manipulated symbols seemed more promising at the time. Logical reasoning was seen as the essence of intelligence, natural or artificial.

Interest in perceptrons, which were invented by Frank Rosenblatt, was kept alive only by the sheer force of his personality.

He predicted optimistically that the perceptron "may eventually be able to learn, make decisions, and translate languages".

Mainstream research into perceptrons ended partly because the 1969 book Perceptrons by Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert emphasized the limits of what perceptrons could do. It was already known that multilayered perceptrons are not subject to the criticism, but nobody in the 1960s knew how to train a multilayered perceptron. Backpropagation was still years away.

It was difficult to find major funding for neural network projects in the 1970s and early 1980s. Important theoretical work still continued even though there was a lack of funding. The "winter" of the neural network approach ended in the middle 1980s, when the work of John Hopfield, David Rumelhart and others revived large scale interest. Rosenblatt did not live to see this, though, since he died in a boating accident shortly after Perceptrons was published.
